questions.question:
D3 — Keep the IDP-call parallelization inside this refactor, or split it into its own change?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Scope Challenge complexity gate, feature cut/deferral 1 of 2.
ELI10: The plan promises "no product behavior change" (PLAN.md:8-9), then proposes firing 5 identity-provider calls at once instead of one after another (PLAN.md:40-41). Going parallel changes real things: the IDP sees 5 simultaneous requests per validation instead of a trickle, which error shows up first changes, and a failure in call 2 no longer prevents calls 3-5 from being sent. If a bug appears after shipping, you cannot tell whether the restructure or the speedup caused it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Bundled, a latency win and a refactor share one blame radius and one rollback; deferred, users keep waiting on 5 serial round-trips a little longer.
Recommendation: B because a refactor that claims zero behavior change should be verifiable as exactly that; the speedup is a 30-minute follow-up with its own tests once the structure lands.
Completeness: A=7/10, B=10/10, C=3/10
Net: one faster PR with mixed blame vs two clean PRs, each provable on its own.

options.label: Split into follow-up PR (recommended)
options.description:
✅ The refactor stays a pure structural change you can diff-test against legacyAuthFlow() behavior
✅ Parallelization lands next with its own error-semantics decision and load test (human: ~half day / CC: ~30 min)
❌ Users wait on 5 serial IDP round-trips for one more release cycle

options.label: Bundle it in this refactor
options.description:
✅ One PR, latency win ships now alongside the reorganization
✅ The IDP client is already being touched, so the edit is cheap (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min)
❌ Mixes a behavior change into a "no behavior change" refactor; regressions become ambiguous to attribute

options.label: Drop it entirely
options.description:
✅ Smallest possible scope for this work; nothing to decide about error semantics
✅ No IDP rate-limit or burst-shape risk introduced
❌ Leaves a known, cheap, measurable latency fix on the floor with no owner

questions.question:
D4 — What happens to `TokenStore`, the new class the plan names but never describes?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Scope Challenge complexity gate, feature cut/deferral 2 of 2.
ELI10: PLAN.md:44-45 lists five new classes. Four are explained somewhere in the plan. `TokenStore` is not: no job, no caller, no relation to `AuthCache`, which already stores tokens keyed by tenant, issuer, audience and policy version (PLAN.md:16-22). In an auth system, an unexplained second place that holds tokens is where stale-token and cross-tenant bugs hide. Either it has a real distinct job that belongs in the plan, or it is a leftover name.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Build it blind and you may ship two token stores with drifting invalidation rules; cut it and it turns out to hold something AuthCache cannot (e.g. refresh tokens or mint receipts), forcing a re-plan.
Recommendation: A because the plan's own contract section says one backing cache; anything TokenStore would do either belongs in AuthCache or has not been justified yet. Re-add it with a written responsibility if a real gap appears.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: remove an undefined moving part now vs carry it forward on faith.

options.label: Cut it from this plan (recommended)
options.description:
✅ One token holder (the existing adapter behind AuthCache), one set of invalidation rules to reason about
✅ Drops the class count to 4 and removes an undefined component from an auth path
❌ If SessionMint needs storage AuthCache cannot offer, it comes back as a re-plan item

options.label: Keep it, but define it before build
options.description:
✅ Preserves the author's intent if TokenStore had a real distinct role (e.g. refresh tokens, mint receipts)
✅ Forces a written responsibility, owner and invalidation contract into the plan before code (human: ~1h / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Keeps a fifth class alive on the assumption a justification exists; blocks Section 1 until it is written

options.label: Hold: discuss before deciding
options.description:
✅ No structural call made without the author's context on what TokenStore was meant to hold
✅ Keeps every other scope answer intact while we talk
❌ Stops the complexity gate here; the review cannot proceed to Section 1 until resolved

questions.question:
D5 — Which class arrangement for the remaining four components (AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy)?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Scope Challenge complexity gate, structure choice. Feature set fixed by D3 (parallelization deferred) and D4 (TokenStore cut).
ELI10: Two of the four remaining classes carry no state. RequestPolicy takes claims plus context and returns allow/deny (PLAN.md:9-13); the author already flags its class boundary as "a proposal to review". AuthCache is a wrapper over an adapter that already does the keying, expiry and invalidation (PLAN.md:16-22). A stateless decision is clearest as a plain exported function. A wrapper is worth keeping only when it narrows a wide adapter to the few calls the services need, which also gives one place to hold the shared-instance decision coming in Section 1. This question picks structure only; how the cache instance is shared, error handling and tests are decided separately.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too many classes means four files to read for one allow/deny decision; too few means AuthBroker and SessionMint each talk to the raw adapter and any future guard (serialization, metrics) lands in two places.
Recommendation: B because RequestPolicy has nothing that needs a class, while AuthCache is the single seam both services share and the natural home for the Section 1 sharing fix.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: fewest files vs one deliberate seam for shared cache access.

options.label: 3 units: keep AuthCache seam, RequestPolicy as function (recommended)
options.description:
✅ AuthBroker + SessionMint + AuthCache classes; RequestPolicy becomes a pure exported decide(claims, ctx) function in its own module, trivially unit-testable
✅ AuthCache stays the one narrow interface both services use, so the Section 1 sharing decision and any future guard live in one place
❌ Still a facade whose only job today is narrowing the adapter API (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)

options.label: 2 classes: drop AuthCache too, services use the adapter directly
options.description:
✅ Fewest moving parts: AuthBroker + SessionMint, RequestPolicy as a function, existing adapter reused as-is
✅ No new cache abstraction to document or keep aligned with the adapter's tests (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min)
❌ Both services depend on the adapter's full surface; a future serialization or tenant-scoping guard must be added in two call sites

options.label: Original 4 classes as planned
options.description:
✅ Matches the author's proposal exactly; RequestPolicy as a class allows later injected policy variants
✅ Uniform shape: every component is a class with the same construction pattern
❌ A class for a stateless allow/deny decision is ceremony; four classes plus 12 files for a no-behavior-change refactor (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~25 min)

questions.question:
D6 — How should AuthBroker and SessionMint get the shared AuthCache instance?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Section 1 Architecture, finding A1 (PLAN.md:28-29).
ELI10: The plan has both services import one cache object from a module and write to it (PLAN.md:28-29). That works until you need two of them: a test that wants a clean cache per case, a second broker for a different tenant pool, or a bundler or test runner that loads the module twice and quietly gives each service a different cache. Handing the cache in through each service's constructor makes the dependency visible and gives you one obvious place (app startup) that owns the single instance.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Tests that pass alone and fail together, or a mint that writes to a cache the broker never reads, both of which look like random auth failures in production.
Recommendation: A because the plan already promises "one backing cache"; constructing it once at startup and injecting it is the standard [Layer 1] way to make that promise true and testable.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10, C=7/10
Net: explicit single ownership at startup vs convenience of a global import.

options.label: Construct once at the composition root, inject into both constructors (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Dependency is explicit in each constructor; a test builds a fresh AuthCache per case with no module reset tricks. ✅ Exactly one instance by construction, so the "one backing cache" contract is enforced where the app boots (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min). ❌ Every place that constructs AuthBroker or SessionMint must now pass the cache; call sites change.

options.label: Keep the module-level exported singleton as planned
options.description: ✅ Zero call-site changes; import and go. ✅ Simplest to write today (human: ~0 / CC: ~0). ❌ Hidden global coupling; test isolation requires jest.resetModules or manual clearing, and duplicate module instances silently split the cache.

options.label: Module export as default, optional constructor override
options.description: ✅ Existing call sites keep working; tests can still inject a fresh instance. ✅ Incremental: can migrate call sites to explicit injection later (human: ~1h / CC: ~5 min). ❌ Two ways to obtain the cache; the default path still hides the dependency and keeps the duplicate-instance risk in production.

answers.D6 \u2014 How should AuthBroker and Sess: Construct once at the composition root, inject into both constructors (recommended)

questions.question:
D7 — How should validateAndDispatch() handle errors?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Section 2 Code Quality, finding C1 (PLAN.md:32-33).
ELI10: The new 60-line function wraps three steps in three nested try/catch blocks, and each catch quietly eats one kind of error (PLAN.md:32-33). In an auth path, a swallowed error is the worst kind: a failed token check or a policy lookup that blew up can fall through and the request gets dispatched anyway, or the user gets a vague failure with nothing in the logs. Three nested blocks also make it hard to see which step a given error belongs to. A flat sequence with one error boundary at the end is shorter, reads top to bottom, and forces every error to become a deliberate outcome.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Fail-open on validation errors (a request proceeds after its check crashed), or hours lost debugging auth failures with no log line.
Recommendation: A because it fixes both problems at once (no swallowing, no nesting) in less code than the plan proposes, and the typed errors double as test seams.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: one explicit error boundary vs three scattered catches vs silence.

options.label: Flat pipeline with typed errors and one boundary mapper (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Every error class maps to an explicit outcome (deny, retryable, internal) and a structured log line with tenant and request id; fail-closed by construction. ✅ Function shrinks to a readable top-to-bottom sequence; each step is independently unit-testable via its thrown error type (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min). ❌ Introduces a small AuthError hierarchy that the codebase must adopt consistently.

options.label: Keep nesting, make every catch explicit (rethrow typed or log + deny)
options.description: ✅ Minimal structural change from the author's draft; keeps step-local handling where it is. ✅ Removes silent swallowing, so no fail-open path remains (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min). ❌ Still 3 levels of nesting in a 60-line function; the error-to-outcome mapping is scattered across three catches instead of one place.

options.label: Keep as planned (each catch swallows its error class)
options.description: ✅ No extra design work; matches the draft exactly. ✅ Fastest to write (human: ~0 / CC: ~0). ❌ Silent failures in an auth path: possible fail-open, no diagnostics, and behavior that no test can pin down.

answers.D7 \u2014 How should validateAndDispatch: Flat pipeline with typed errors and one boundary mapper (recommended)

questions.question:
D8 — How do we prove the rewritten legacyAuthFlow() still behaves exactly as before?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Section 3 Test review, finding T1 (PLAN.md:36-37, :23-25). This is the mandatory regression contract; the question is how to cover it, not whether.
ELI10: The whole point of this plan is "same behavior, better structure" (PLAN.md:8-9), yet the plan rewrites legacyAuthFlow() with no test that pins down what it does today (PLAN.md:36-37). Without that, "same behavior" is a hope. The standard move is to write characterization tests first: feed the old code every kind of request it handles today, record what it does, then run the exact same tests against the new AuthBroker path. Green means parity. A thin shim that keeps existing callers on the old entry point until parity is green means nothing user-facing changes until it is proven.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A tenant that used to be denied gets allowed (or the reverse) and nobody knows until a customer reports it; a refactor becomes an auth incident.
Recommendation: A because with CC the full characterization suite costs minutes, and it is the only option that turns "no behavior change" into a checked claim rather than an assertion.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=10/10 (C adds runtime verification on top of A, not more test coverage)
Net: proven parity with a reversible switch vs sampling the happy paths vs production-grade verification.

options.label: Full characterization suite + compatibility shim until parity (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Every observable legacy outcome (allow, deny, expired, revoked, suspended tenant, IDP error, malformed claims, cache hit/miss, logout invalidation) is recorded as input → outcome and replayed against the new path. ✅ Callers stay on legacyAuthFlow() through a shim until the suite is green, so the cutover is a one-line, reversible switch (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min). ❌ Requires enumerating legacy callers and behaviors up front; the suite is throwaway-adjacent once parity lands (keep it as the regression suite).

options.label: Parity tests for the top ~5 paths, no shim
options.description: ✅ Covers the paths users hit most; fast to write (human: ~3h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ No shim means fewer moving parts during cutover. ❌ Rare paths (suspended tenant, malformed claims, invalidation races) are exactly where auth regressions hide; a cutover with no fallback switch.

options.label: A plus flag-gated shadow compare in production
options.description: ✅ Catches behaviors the suite author did not think of by diffing old vs new outcomes on real traffic. ✅ Zero user impact while shadowing: old path serves, new path only logs (human: ~2.5 days / CC: ~45 min). ❌ Doubles IDP load during shadow, needs a flag system and mismatch dashboard; heavier than a structural refactor warrants.

answers.D8 \u2014 How do we prove the rewritten: Full characterization suite + compatibility shim until parity (recommended)

questions.question:
D9 — How deep should tests go for the new components beyond success/error paths?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Section 3 Test review, finding T2 (PLAN.md:23-24).
ELI10: The plan promises tests for the new pieces when things work and when they fail (PLAN.md:23-24). That misses the cases multi-tenant auth actually breaks on: a token from tenant A being served to tenant B, a token that expires at exactly this second, a policy version bump that should make old cache entries invisible, a session minted a moment after the tenant was suspended. Each of those is a five-line test once the components exist. The regression suite (D8), error-mapping tests (D7) and injection test (D6) are already required; this decides the extra edge-case and end-to-end layer.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Cross-tenant leakage or a resurrected revoked token, found by a customer instead of a test.
Recommendation: A because these edge cases are the actual failure modes of tenant auth and cost minutes with CC.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: prove the failure modes that matter in multi-tenant auth vs the minimum the plan states.

options.label: Full edge-case + E2E coverage (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Pins down tenant isolation, expiry boundary, policy-version bump, malformed claims, mint-after-invalidation and fail-closed on unknown errors. ✅ Four E2E flows (valid / expired / revoked / suspended) plus IDP-down prove the whole path, not just units (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min). ❌ Larger test file count to maintain; E2E flows need a fake IDP or recorded fixtures.

options.label: Success/error paths as planned
options.description: ✅ Matches the author's stated plan; smaller test surface to write and maintain. ✅ Fast (human: ~3h / CC: ~8 min). ❌ Leaves the tenant-isolation and invalidation-race cases, the ones that cause auth incidents, unproven.

D11 — TODO: confirm the adapter's invalidation-vs-write ordering when two services mutate one cache?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Final planning decisions, TODO candidate 2 of 2 (from Architecture finding 2, medium confidence 5/10).

Why: it decides whether the D9 "mint after invalidation does not resurrect" test passes for free or needs a guard in AuthCache. Pros: settles a fail-open risk with a 30-minute read. Cons: may find nothing. Context: read the adapter's invalidate and set paths plus their tests. Depends on: nothing; can run before implementation starts.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skip it and the D9 test is the first place anyone learns the answer, possibly mid-implementation.
Recommendation: A because it is cheap, bounded, and directly de-risks an approved test.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

## Architecture

```
                          composition root (bootstrap)
                          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                          │ adapter = existingCacheAdapter│
                          │ cache   = new AuthCache(adapter)   (one instance, D6)
                          │ broker  = new AuthBroker({ cache, idpClient, dispatcher })
                          │ mint    = new SessionMint({ cache, idpClient })
                          └───────────┬───────────┬──────┘
                                      │           │
   request ──► legacyAuthFlow() shim ─┤           │
              (delegates to old impl  │           │
               until D8 suite green,  ▼           ▼
               then to broker)   AuthBroker    SessionMint
                                      │             │ set(tenantKey, session)
   validateAndDispatch(req):          │             ▼
     1. claims = validate(token)  ────┼──► AuthCache (facade) ──► existing adapter
        cache.get(tenantKey) hit? ────┘    get / set / invalidate     keys: tenant, issuer,
        miss → idpClient (5 serial calls,                            audience, policyVersion
               unchanged in this PR)                                 evicts expired; hooks on
     2. decision = decide(claims, ctx)   ← pure fn, no I/O           logout / revoke / suspend
     3. deny → PolicyDeniedError                                     (unchanged, tests retained)
        allow → dispatcher.dispatch(req)
     catch (e) → mapAuthError(e) → { outcome, log(tenantId, requestId) }
```

### Error boundary (D7)
```
TokenValidationError ─► deny (401-class)        ─┐
PolicyDeniedError    ─► deny (403-class)          ├─► one structured log line
IdpUnavailableError  ─► retryable (503-class)     │   { tenantId, requestId, errorClass }
DispatchError        ─► internal                  │
unknown              ─► internal + deny (closed) ─┘
```
No catch swallows. Unknown classes fail closed.

### Component contracts
- **AuthCache** (`auth/AuthCache.ts`): narrow facade exposing only `get`, `set`, `invalidate` over the existing adapter. Retains keying (tenant ID, issuer, audience, policy version), expiry eviction and invalidation hooks unchanged (PLAN.md:16-22). No module-level export. Constructor takes the adapter.
- **decide(claims, ctx)** (`auth/requestPolicy.ts`): pure; returns allow/deny under the existing access policy; missing or malformed claims → deny (matches legacy).
- **AuthBroker** (`auth/AuthBroker.ts`): constructor `{ cache, idpClient, dispatcher }`; `validateAndDispatch(req)` as diagrammed. Cache hit short-circuits all IDP calls.
- **SessionMint** (`auth/SessionMint.ts`): constructor `{ cache, idpClient }`; writes through AuthCache only.
- **Shim**: `legacyAuthFlow()` keeps its signature; body delegates to the old implementation until the characterization suite passes on `AuthBroker`, then delegates to the broker (one-line, reversible).
- **AuthError hierarchy** (`auth/errors.ts`): `AuthError` base; `TokenValidationError`, `PolicyDeniedError`, `IdpUnavailableError`, `DispatchError`; `mapAuthError()` in `auth/AuthBroker.ts` or `auth/errors.ts`.
